---
title: "Exercise: intensity inside an object"
---

## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- compute the **intensity statistics** of an object by hand: integrated, mean, median, quartiles, MAD, edge-band mean,
- predict which of them change under a **background offset**, a **gain**, a **mask error** and **saturation**,
- compute an **intensity-weighted centroid** and the **mass displacement**,
- assign pixels to **radial rings** and compute FracAtD and MeanFrac,
- normalise well values with a **z-score** and a **robust z-score**, and say when that is not enough.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo.

## Background

| Idea | What it means |
|---|---|
| Integrated intensity | the sum of the pixel values of the object: the amount of dye |
| Mean | sum / number of pixels: the concentration |
| Median, quartiles | sort the $n$ values; the value at position $h = (n-1)p$ (counting from 0), interpolating between neighbours; $p = 0.5$, $0.25$, $0.75$ |
| MAD | the median of the distances $|I - \text{median}|$ |
| Edge band | object pixels with a 4-neighbour outside the object (object minus its erosion by the cross) |
| Mass displacement | distance between the geometric centroid and the intensity-weighted centroid |
| Radial position | $\rho = d_c / (d_c + d_e)$: $d_c$ to the centre, $d_e$ to the edge; $k$ rings of equal width in $\rho$ |
| FracAtD, MeanFrac | share of the intensity in a ring; that share divided by the ring's share of the pixels |
| Robust z | $(x - \text{median of controls}) / (1.4826 \cdot \text{MAD of controls})$ |

Standard deviations of pixel values divide by $n$; the z-score of wells uses the usual sample standard deviation ($n - 1$).

## By hand

The object is the whole $5 \times 5$ block below (on a dark background); $x$ is the column (0–4, left to right), $y$ the row (0–4, top to bottom).

$$I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 & 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 8 & 6 \\ 2 & 3 & 5 & 9 & 7 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

**B1.** (a) Compute the integrated intensity, the mean, the minimum and the maximum.
(b) Sort the 25 values. Give the median and the lower and upper quartiles. (With $n = 25$ the positions $h$ are whole numbers.)
(c) Compute the MAD.

**B2.** The edge band is the outer ring of 16 pixels.
(a) Compute the edge mean and the mean of the inner $3 \times 3$ pixels.
(b) Compute edge / mean. Is this cell rim-stained?

**B3.** The camera adds a constant background of 10 to every pixel.
(a) Without recomputing everything, give the new integrated intensity, mean, median, MAD and standard deviation (the old one is 2.12).
(b) Compute the new edge / mean. Why did it move towards 1?
(c) Instead of the offset, the gain doubles. Which of the numbers of B1 and B2 change, and how?

**B4.** The segmentation is one pixel too large: the object is now the $7 \times 7$ block with a border of background pixels of value 1 around $I$. Compute the new mean and median. Which of the two is hurt more, and why?

**B5.** (a) Compute the geometric centroid. (b) The column sums of $I$ are 8, 13, 16, 26, 18 and the row sums 8, 14, 23, 26, 10. Compute the intensity-weighted centroid. (c) Compute the mass displacement. In which direction is the signal displaced?

**B6.** Radial rings ($k = 3$).
(a) Three pixels have $(d_c, d_e) = (1, 4)$, $(3, 3)$ and $(5, 1)$. Compute $\rho$ for each and the ring it falls in.
(b) A small object has 2 pixels of value 10 in ring 1, 3 pixels of value 6 in ring 2 and 5 pixels of value 2 in ring 3. Compute FracAtD and MeanFrac for each ring. Where is the signal enriched?

**B7.** A feature of five control wells: 98, 102, 100, 95, 130. Five treated wells: 101, 140, 99, 160, 120.
(a) Compute the mean and sample standard deviation of the controls, and the z-score of each treated well. Which wells have $|z| > 3$?
(b) Compute the median and MAD of the controls, and the robust z of each treated well. Which wells have $|z| > 3$ now?
(c) Why do the two answers differ?

### Math questions

**B8.** *(math)* Show that for $J = gI + b$ ($g > 0$) every quantile satisfies $q_p(J) = g\,q_p(I) + b$, that $\mathrm{MAD}(J) = g\,\mathrm{MAD}(I)$, and that a ratio of two means $\mu_1/\mu_2$ is unchanged by $g$ but not by $b$.

**B9.** *(math)* Show that the intensity-weighted centroid of a uniform object coincides with its geometric centroid, and that it does too for any intensity that is symmetric under a point reflection through the geometric centroid ($I(2\bar{\mathbf x} - \mathbf x) = I(\mathbf x)$, object symmetric as well).

**B10.** *(math)* For normal data with standard deviation $\sigma$, show that the MAD tends to $\sigma\,\Phi^{-1}(3/4)$, and hence that $1.4826 \cdot \mathrm{MAD}$ estimates $\sigma$.

**B11.** *(math)* Show that $\sum_j a_j\,\mathrm{MeanFrac}_j = 1$ for the rings of an object ($a_j$ = share of the pixels in ring $j$), and that $\mathrm{MeanFrac}_j$ equals the ring's mean intensity divided by the object's mean intensity.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**B1.** (a) Integrated 81, mean $81/25 = 3.24$, min 1, max 9.
(b) Sorted: 1 1 1 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 3 3 3 3 3 4 4 5 6 7 8 9. Median: position 12 → **2**. Lower quartile: position 6 → **2**. Upper quartile: position 18 → **4**.
(c) Distances from the median 2, sorted: ten 0s, eight 1s, then 2 2 3 4 5 6 7. The median (position 12) is **1**: MAD = 1.

**B2.** (a) Edge ring: $1+2+2+2+1$ (top) $+ 1+2+2+3+2$ (bottom) $+ 2+2+2$ (left, rows 1–3) $+ 2+6+7$ (right) $= 39$ over 16 pixels: **2.44**. Inner $3 \times 3$: $3+3+4+3+4+8+3+5+9 = 42$, mean **4.67**.
(b) Edge / mean $= 2.44/3.24 = 0.75$. Below 1: the edge is darker than the average, so not rim-stained (a rim-stained cell has edge / mean > 1).

**B3.** (a) Integrated $81 + 25 \cdot 10 = 331$, mean 13.24, median 12, MAD 1 (unchanged), standard deviation 2.12 (unchanged).
(b) $(2.44 + 10)/(3.24 + 10) = 12.44/13.24 = 0.94$. The offset is added to both means; a ratio $(a+b)/(c+b)$ tends to 1 as $b$ grows. Subtract the background before forming ratios.
(c) Integrated, mean, min, max, median, quartiles, MAD, standard deviation and the edge mean all double (162, 6.48, …, MAD 2, sd 4.24). Edge / mean stays 0.75: the gain cancels in a ratio.

**B4.** The $7 \times 7$ block has 49 pixels and sum $81 + 24 \cdot 1 = 105$: mean $105/49 = 2.14$ (was 3.24, −34 %). Sorted, the 49 values start with $3 + 24 = 27$ ones, so the median (position 24) is **1** (was 2). Here the median is hurt more: the added background pixels are now the majority of the dark values. In a large object the extra ring is a small fraction of the pixels; the median then hardly moves while the mean still drops (demo: uniform cell, mask 2 px too large, median unchanged at 112.1, mean 110.0 → 104.3).

**B5.** (a) $(\bar x, \bar y) = (2, 2)$.
(b) $\bar x_I = (0\cdot8 + 1\cdot13 + 2\cdot16 + 3\cdot26 + 4\cdot18)/81 = 195/81 = 2.41$; $\bar y_I = (0\cdot8 + 1\cdot14 + 2\cdot23 + 3\cdot26 + 4\cdot10)/81 = 178/81 = 2.20$.
(c) $\sqrt{0.41^2 + 0.20^2} = 0.45$ px, towards the right and down: the bright pixels 8, 9, 7, 6 sit in the lower right.

**B6.** (a) $\rho = 1/5 = 0.2$ → ring 1; $3/6 = 0.5$ → ring 2 ($[1/3, 2/3)$); $5/6 = 0.83$ → ring 3.
(b) Total $20 + 18 + 10 = 48$. FracAtD $= 20/48, 18/48, 10/48 = 0.417, 0.375, 0.208$. Pixel shares $2/10, 3/10, 5/10$. MeanFrac $= 2.08, 1.25, 0.42$: enriched in the centre, depleted at the edge (a "nuclear" pattern).

**B7.** (a) Mean 105, sd 14.21. $z$ = −0.28, **2.46**, −0.42, **3.87**, 1.06: only the well with 160 passes $|z| > 3$.
(b) Median 100; distances 2, 2, 0, 5, 30, median **2**; scale $1.4826 \cdot 2 = 2.97$. Robust $z$ = 0.34, **13.5**, −0.34, **20.2**, **6.7**: three wells (140, 160, 120) pass.
(c) The control 130 is an outlier. It pulls the mean up and inflates the sd from about 3 to 14, so real effects look small. The median and MAD ignore it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (math)"}
**B8.** $x \mapsto gx + b$ is strictly increasing, so it keeps the order of the sorted values; the value at position $h$ (and any interpolation between two neighbours, being linear) maps to $g\,q_p + b$. Then $|J_k - q_{0.5}(J)| = g\,|I_k - q_{0.5}(I)|$, and the median of these is $g\,\mathrm{MAD}(I)$. Means: $\mu_i(J) = g\mu_i + b$, so $\frac{g\mu_1 + b}{g\mu_2 + b}$ equals $\mu_1/\mu_2$ for $b = 0$ (any $g$) but not in general for $b \ne 0$.

**B9.** With $I = c$: $\sum I\mathbf x / \sum I = c\sum \mathbf x / (c\,n) = \bar{\mathbf x}$. With point symmetry, pair each pixel $\mathbf x$ with $\mathbf x' = 2\bar{\mathbf x} - \mathbf x$ (also in the object, same intensity): $I(\mathbf x)\mathbf x + I(\mathbf x')\mathbf x' = 2I(\mathbf x)\bar{\mathbf x}$. Summing over all pairs gives $\sum I\mathbf x = \bar{\mathbf x}\sum I$.

**B10.** For $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ the median is $\mu$, and the MAD is the median $m$ of $|X - \mu|$: $P(|X - \mu| \le m) = 2\Phi(m/\sigma) - 1 = 1/2$, so $\Phi(m/\sigma) = 3/4$ and $m = \sigma\,\Phi^{-1}(3/4) = 0.6745\,\sigma$. The sample MAD converges to $m$, and $1/0.6745 = 1.4826$.

**B11.** $\sum_j a_j\,\mathrm{MeanFrac}_j = \sum_j \mathrm{FracAtD}_j = 1$. And $\mathrm{FracAtD}_j / a_j = \dfrac{S_j / S}{n_j / n} = \dfrac{S_j/n_j}{S/n} = \bar I_j / \bar I$, with $S_j, n_j$ the ring's sum and pixel count.
:::

## Explore {#explore}

The demo measures one synthetic cell. All six patterns have the **same mask** (6521 pixels) and the **same total signal** (mean 100). Sliders change the acquisition (background **offset**, **gain**, **noise**, **saturation** level) and the **mask** (grown or shrunk by up to 2 pixels), and the number of **rings**. The image shows the mask outline (yellow), the edge band (cyan), the rings (alternating tints), the geometric centroid (white +) and the intensity-weighted centroid (red dot), joined by the mass-displacement arrow. The histogram shows the values inside the mask with the mean (blue) and the median and quartiles (red). The table gives every feature and its change **Δ** against the ideal measurement of the same cell (no offset, gain 1, no noise, no saturation, exact mask). The tabs **population** and **plate** are used in E7–E9.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="intensityfeat" data-preset="offset"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/intensityfeat.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Preset **background offset** (offset 40, noise σ = 4). Which features moved by about 40, which by about $40 \cdot 6521$, and which hardly moved? Why did std and MAD change a little at all?

**E2.** Preset **same integral, other pattern**, then click through the six patterns. Check that the integrated intensity and the mean never change. Which single column best separates uniform from punctate? Uniform from gradient? Which pattern has the same FracAtD as the uniform cell, and which column tells them apart?

**E3.** Preset **rim vs filled**. Note edge / mean. Now shrink the mask by 1 and by 2 pixels, then grow it by 1. What happens to edge / mean, and why is it so sensitive?

**E4.** Preset **polarised cell**. Read the mass displacement. Add an offset of 50: what happens to it, and why? Then tick "rings around the intensity maximum" with 4 rings: compare MeanFrac of ring 1 with the centroid-centred rings.

**E5.** Preset **nuclear: radial bins**. Read MeanFrac for the 4 rings. Try 2 and 8 rings. Add an offset of 50; then instead set the gain to 2. Which of the two changes MeanFrac?

**E6.** Preset **dilated mask** (offset 10, mask +2 px) and then **saturation**. For each, which columns are wrong, by how much, and in which direction?

**E7.** Tab **population** (or preset **two cell types**): 10 cells of type A and 10 of type B, with different brightness. Plot mean against std. Which feature separates the types, which does not? Try area against integrated intensity.

**E8.** Preset **plate offset: robust z**. First choose normalisation **none**: compare the control wells of plate A and plate B. Then **robust z**: how many treated wells (marked *) pass $|z| > 3$ on each plate, and how many other wells?

**E9.** Preset **plate gradient hides it** (gradient 12 per column, robust z). How many treated wells pass $|z| > 3$ now, and why? Switch to **row/col + robust z**. Then set the gradient back to 0 and compare.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** Mean (100 → 140.1), median (102.1 → 141.6) and the quartiles (138.4 and 144.5) moved by about 40; the max moved more (to 156.1), because the noise adds to the extremes; the integrated intensity by about $40 \cdot 6521 = 260\,840$ (652 100 → 913 293). The std moved only from 7.6 to 8.7 and the MAD from 0 to 3.1: an offset does not change the spread, but the noise (σ = 4) does add spread. Edge / mean moved from 0.66 to 0.75, towards 1.

**E2.** Integrated 652 100 and mean 100.0 for all six. Uniform against punctate: the std (7.6 against 82.0) or the max (102 against 559). Uniform against gradient: the std (7.6 against 41.8), the MAD (0 against 33.6), or the mass displacement (0 against 10.6 px). The gradient has the same FracAtD as the uniform cell (0.058, 0.190, 0.325, 0.426), because a linear ramp adds as much on one side of each ring as it removes on the other; RadialCV tells them apart (0.08 to 0.48 against 0).

**E3.** Edge / mean 2.43 with the exact mask. Shrinking by 1 px: 3.27; by 2 px: 3.58; growing by 1 px: 1.34. The rim is only a few pixels wide, and the edge band is one pixel: moving the mask by one pixel moves the band to a different place on the steep intensity profile of the rim (and the mean changes too: 100 → 94.1 → 85.1 when shrinking). Edge features need an accurate mask.

**E4.** Mass displacement 8.88 px. With offset 50: 5.92 px. The offset adds the same value to every pixel, which pulls the weighted centroid towards the geometric one (a uniform object has displacement 0). With rings around the intensity maximum, ring 1 now sits on the spot: MeanFrac 4.07, 1.66, 0.85, 0.68 (centroid-centred: 0.81, 1.19, 1.23, 0.78, which shows the spot only as enrichment in the middle rings).

**E5.** MeanFrac 3.26, 2.62, 0.45, 0.42. With 2 rings: 2.77, 0.43; with 8: 3.26, 3.26, 3.26, 2.17, 0.45, 0.44, 0.44, 0.40 (the boundary of the bright region falls inside ring 4). The offset changes MeanFrac (2.51, 2.08, 0.63, 0.61: towards 1); the gain does not (it cancels in the ratio).

**E6.** **Dilated mask**: the mean drops from 110.0 to 104.3 (and the integrated intensity rises from 717 310 to 735 400: 528 extra pixels of blurred edge and background), the std jumps from 7.6 to 21.5, edge / mean falls from 0.69 to 0.22; the median (112.1) does not move. **Saturation** (spot cell clipped at 300): the max is 300 instead of 488.4, the mean 96.0 instead of 100.0, the integrated intensity 4 % too low, the std 62.7 instead of 77.7, and the mass displacement 8.12 instead of 8.88 px; median and quartiles are unchanged (only the brightest pixels are clipped).

**E7.** The mean overlaps completely (type A 84–123, type B 81–124): brightness varies within both types. The std separates them cleanly (A: 8.9–11.5, B: 56–90): punctate staining has a wide spread of values. Area also separates them, just (A 3063–4439 px, B 2131–2995 px), and integrated intensity mixes size and brightness, so the types overlap there.

**E8.** Without normalisation the controls of plate A lie between 94 and 103, those of plate B between 149 and 169: the same treatment would give different numbers on the two plates. With robust z all four treated wells pass $|z| > 3$ on both plates (z 10.1–12.6 on A, 4.4–6.1 on B) and no other well does.

**E9.** None: the gradient spreads the controls (64 to 133 on plate A), so their MAD and the robust scale grow, and the treated wells reach only $z$ = 0.4 to 1.4. Robust z corrects an offset and a gain, not a trend across the plate. With the row/column correction all four treated wells come back ($z$ 6.8–9.8 on plate A) and no other well passes. With gradient 0 robust z alone was enough.
:::

## Where this leads

The intensity statistics treat the pixels of an object as a bag of values: they ignore how the values are arranged. The next unit, **texture**, looks at **pairs** of pixels: the co-occurrence matrix and the features computed from it. Later on, the feature table is the input of the random forests day (classifying objects) and of the evaluation day (turning measurements into claims).
